How uncertainty works in cosm.py
The file does forward uncertainty propagation by plain Monte Carlo sampling. In order:

1. Representing uncertainty (cosm.py:27-48). Each uncertain quantity is a parametric distribution, either Normal(mean, sd) or Uniform(lo, hi). A plain number counts as a distribution with zero spread (_sampler). Both model parameters (params=) and caller-supplied inputs (run(co2=Normal(560, 20))) can be uncertain.

2. Sampling (cosm.py:128-146). run(n=…) draws n independent samples for every free input and every parameter. Each step's function is then evaluated n times, once per sample index i. Every port's values are stored as a length-n list in env.

3. Dependence is carried by index. This is the part that makes it correct. Sample i of dT is computed from sample i of co2 and S. Sample i of yield_change then uses that same dT[i]. So each index is one consistent draw from the joint distribution of the whole pipeline. Correlations created by the model's structure survive: if two outputs both depend on dT, they stay correlated. It is equivalent to running the whole composed function n times, just organised step by step.

4. Seeding (cosm.py:131-139). Each input and each step gets its own RNG, seeded from a string like "42:warming". Adding or reordering steps therefore doesn't change the draws of existing ones. This is essentially common random numbers: when you compare two model variants, the differences come from the change you made, not from sampling noise.

5. Summarising (cosm.py:199-203). For each port it reports the mean and a 90% interval taken from the 5th and 95th percentiles of the samples.

6. Checks as probabilities (cosm.py:162-164). A check is a predicate over ports, evaluated on every sample. The result is a pass rate rather than true/false, i.e. an estimate of P(constraint holds).

Is it standard?
The core is very standard. Monte Carlo forward propagation with independent input distributions is the textbook baseline:

It is essentially what the metrology standard GUM Supplement 1 (JCGM 101:2008), "propagation of distributions using a Monte Carlo method", prescribes.
It is how Guesstimate, Squiggle, Analytica and @Risk/Crystal Ball work. Guesstimate also uses 90% intervals by default, so the reporting style matches that tradition.
Using quantile intervals instead of mean ± k·sd is good practice, because outputs here can be skewed. Dividing by Uniform(0.2, 0.6) in the example gives a heavy right tail.
Somewhat less common, but sensible:

Stable per-component seed streams. Most tools use one global stream, so adding a node reshuffles every draw. This design is closer to what careful simulation practitioners do by hand.
Reporting checks as pass rates. This matches the "probability of failure" idea from reliability engineering. Simple propagation tools rarely make it first-class.
What's missing compared with fuller UQ practice
These are gaps, not mistakes, for a seed design:

Every distribution is independent. You can't say two parameters are correlated (no copulas, joint distributions or correlation matrices). Related, and easy to miss: a parameter is private to its step. If two steps each declare a parameter S, they get independent draws, even if they mean the same physical constant. A shared uncertain quantity has to be routed through as an input instead.
No split between aleatory and epistemic uncertainty. Real variability and lack of knowledge are mixed in one sampling loop. The standard way to keep them apart is nested ("two-loop") Monte Carlo, or imprecise probabilities such as p-boxes and intervals.
Forward only, no calibration. Distributions are priors set by hand. Nothing updates them against data, as Bayesian calibration or Kennedy–O'Hagan would.
No sensitivity analysis. Nothing says which parameter drives the output spread. Sobol indices or simple rank correlations would be the usual addition, and the per-index samples already make the latter cheap.
No check on Monte Carlo error. There is no standard error, convergence check or adaptive n. The 5%/95% tails are the noisiest estimates. GUM-S1 includes an adaptive procedure for exactly this.
Plain random sampling. Latin hypercube or quasi-Monte Carlo (Sobol sequences) would get the same accuracy with fewer runs. That matters once steps are expensive.
Uncertainty about the model itself is text only. assumptions are recorded strings and don't enter the numbers. There is no ensemble over alternative model structures. That is common, but it's worth noting given the project's audit goals.
Distributions can go outside physical limits. Normal can produce negative values for quantities that must be positive. The checks mechanism will reveal this after the run but won't prevent it. Truncated or lognormal distributions are the usual fix.
In short: the method is standard Monte Carlo propagation, done cleanly. Pairing samples by index keeps the joint distribution correct through composition, and the seeding is more careful than most simple tools manage. Its main departure from fuller UQ practice is assuming every distribution is independent. Parameters private to each step, which can't be shared across steps, are the gap most likely to matter as models are composed across disciplines.
